This is a Meccan surah without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Inshiqaq was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh related a similar report from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Rafi', who said: "I prayed the 'atamah (night) prayer behind Abu Hurayrah, and he recited ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and prostrated. I said to him, and he said: 'I prostrated behind Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ), and I will not stop prostrating in it until I meet him.'"

Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq].

Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Ruwayani in his Musnad, and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Buraydah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the noon prayer ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and similar surahs."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ is like His saying ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], in whether the verb is supplied or not.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: its splitting is one of the signs of the Resurrection, and the meaning of its splitting is its cleaving with white clouds, as in His saying ﴿and the day the sky is split open with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It was also said that it splits from the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is the gate of the sky.

Scholars differed about the answer (jawab) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). al-Farra' said that it is "adhinat" (it listened), and the waw is extra, and likewise "alqat" (it cast out). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the Arabs do not insert a waw except with ﴿hatta idha﴾ (until when), as in His saying ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and with ﴿lamma﴾ (when), as in His saying ﴿So when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead, and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104]; it is not inserted with anything other than these two.

It was said that the answer is His saying ﴿fa-mulaqihi﴾ (then you will meet it), meaning ﴿fa-anta mulaqihi﴾ (then you are one who will meet it), and this is the view of al-Akhfash.

al-Mubarrad said: In the speech there is a transposition, meaning ﴿O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet it﴾ ﴿when the sky splits open﴾.

al-Mubarrad also said: The answer is His saying ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾, and this is the view of al-Kisa'i. The construction is: ﴿when the sky splits open﴾, then whoever is given his record in his right hand, his ruling is such-and-such. It was also said that it is ﴿O mankind﴾ with the fa' (then) elided. It was said that it is ﴿O mankind﴾ with the saying elided, meaning it will be said to him, "O mankind." It was also said that the answer is omitted, its estimate being "you will be resurrected," or "every person will meet his deed." It was also said that it is what was stated in Surat al-Takwir, meaning "a soul will know this," on the assumption that ﴿idha﴾ is conditional. It was also said that it is not conditional, and it is governed by a deleted verb, meaning "remember," or it is a subject whose predicate is the second ﴿idha﴾, with the waw extra, and the estimate is: the time of the splitting of the sky is the time of the stretching of the earth.

The meaning of ﴿and it listened to its Lord﴾ is that it obeyed Him in splitting, from "idhn," which is listening to a thing and giving ear to it. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, meaning it is right for it to obey, submit and listen. Among the uses of "idhn" for listening is the poet's saying:

"Deaf, when they hear good said of me, and if I am mentioned with evil in their presence, they listen (adhinu)."

And the saying of another:

"If they listen to a doubt, they fly with it, rejoicing at me; and what they listen to of good is buried."

It was also said that the meaning is: Allah made it certain that it would listen to His command to split, meaning He made it fit for that.

al-Dahhak said: "Haqqat" means "it obeyed," and "it is right for it to obey its Lord because He created it." One says, "So-and-so is entitled (mahquq) to such-and-such." The meaning of its obedience is that it does not refuse what Allah wills for it.

Qatadah said: "It is right for it (haqqa laha) to do that." From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"If there is reproach, then welcome and hail; and reproach is due to her from us, and it has become scarce."

And ﴿when the earth is stretched out﴾, meaning spread out as hide is spread, and its mountains are leveled until it becomes a level plain in which you see no crookedness or elevation.

Muqatil said: It is made level like the stretching of a hide, so no building or mountain remains on it except that it enters into it. It was also said: "It is stretched" means its extent is increased, from "madad," which is increase.

﴿And it casts out what is in it﴾, meaning it brings out what is in it of the dead and the treasures, and throws them onto its surface, and empties itself of them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It casts out what is in its belly of the dead, and empties itself of those who are on its back of the living. Similar to this is His saying ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2].

﴿And it listened to its Lord﴾, meaning it heard and obeyed what He commanded it of casting out and emptying itself. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, meaning it was made fit for listening to that and submitting to it. The meaning of the two verbs has already been explained before this.

﴿O mankind﴾: the intended meaning is the human species, so it includes the believer and the disbeliever. It was also said that it refers only to the disbelieving human. The first is preferable because of the detail that will come. ﴿Indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil﴾. In the speech of the Arabs, "kadh" (toil) is striving at a thing with effort, without distinction between that thing being good or bad. The meaning is: indeed you are striving toward your Lord in your deed, or toward meeting your Lord. It is derived from "kadaha jildahu," meaning when he scratched his skin.

Ibn Muqbil said:

"Time is only two turns: in one of them I die, and in the other I seek life, toiling."

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: "Working for your Lord a work, then you will meet it," meaning you will meet your deed. The meaning is that you will inevitably meet the reward of your deed and what follows from it of reward and punishment.

al-Qutaybi said: The meaning of the verse is: indeed you are laboring, that is, working and toiling in your livelihood, toward the meeting with your Lord. "Mulaqah" means "liqa'," that is, you will meet your Lord with your deed. It was also said: "fa-mulaqin" means you will meet the book of your deed, because the deed has already ended.

﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾, and they are the believers.

﴿He will be brought to a reckoning that is easy﴾, one in which there is no scrutiny.

Muqatil said: Because his sins will be forgiven and he will not be brought to account for them.

The exegetes said: It is that his evil deeds are shown to him, then Allah forgives them, and that is the easy reckoning.

﴿And he will return to his people in happiness﴾, meaning after the easy reckoning he will return to his people who are in Paradise from among his kin, or to his people who were with him in the world of wives and children and who had preceded him to Paradise, or to those whom Allah has prepared for him in Paradise of the dark-eyed maidens (hur 'in) and the eternal youths, or to all of these, happy, rejoicing in what he has been given of goodness and honor.

﴿But as for he who is given his record behind his back﴾. al-Kalbi said: Because his right hand will be chained to his neck, and his left hand will be behind him.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: The bones and the plates of his chest will be unlocked, then his hand will enter and come out from his back, and he will take his record in that manner.

﴿He will call for destruction﴾, meaning when he reads his record he will say, "Woe to me! Destruction to me!" And "thubur" is ruin.

﴿And he will burn in the Blaze﴾, meaning he will enter it and suffer its heat and its severity.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and 'Asim read with a fat-hah on the ya' (yaṣla), a sukun on the sad and a light lam.

The rest read with a damma on the ya' and a fat-hah on the lam, with a shaddah. Isma'il al-Makki related from Ibn Kathir, and likewise Kharijah from Nafi', and likewise Isma'il al-Makki related from Ibn Kathir that they read with a damma on the ya' and a sukun on the sad, from "asla, yuslī."

﴿Indeed, he was among his people, happy﴾, meaning he was among his people in the world, happy in following his desire and indulging his lust, insolent and arrogant, because the Hereafter did not occur to his mind. The clause is a reason for what precedes it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return﴾ is a reason for his having been happy among his people in the world. The meaning is: the cause of that happiness was his supposing that he would not return to Allah and would not be raised for reckoning and punishment, because he denied the resurrection and rejected the Hereafter. The "an" in His saying ﴿an lan yahur﴾ (that he would never return) is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," which, with what follows it, takes the place of the two objects of "thanna" (supposed). "Haur" in language means return; one says "haara, yahuru" when he returns. al-Raghib said: "haur" is hesitation in a matter, and from it is the saying: "We seek refuge in Allah from haur after kawr," meaning from hesitation in a matter after proceeding in it. "Muhawarat al-kalam" is responding to speech, and "mahar" is the place of return and destination.

'Ikrimah and Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: "Yahur" is a word in Abyssinian, and its meaning is "return."

al-Qurtubi said: "Haur" in the speech of the Arabs is return, and from it is his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from haur after kawr," meaning from returning to deficiency after increase. Likewise "huur" with a damma. In the proverb: "haur in mahar," meaning a deficiency within a deficiency. From it is the saying of the poet:

"The blood is being poured out, and the people's return is in haur."

"Huur" is also destruction, and from it is the saying of the reciter:

"In a well of no haur he went, and he did not perceive."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: meaning "in a well of haur," and "la" is extra.

﴿Yes, indeed his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾. "Bala" is an affirmation of what was negated by "lan": meaning, yes, he will certainly return and will certainly be raised.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿indeed his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾, meaning He was aware of him and of his deeds, and nothing of them was hidden from Him.

al-Zajjaj said: "Kana bihi basiran" means He was seeing of him before He created him, knowing that his return was to Him.

﴿So I swear by the twilight﴾. The "la" is extra, as has been mentioned before in similar expressions, and we have already mentioned the disagreement about it in Surat al-Qiyamah, so refer back to it. "Ash-shafaq" is the redness that appears after the sun sets until the time of the late night prayer ('isha').

al-Wahidi said: This is the view of the exegetes and the lexicographers all together.

al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs say: "He has a dyed garment, as if it were the shafaq," and it was red. This is related by al-Qurtubi from most of the Companions, the Successors and the jurists.

Asad ibn 'Amr and Abu Hanifah, in one of the two reports from him, said: It is the whiteness. There is no basis for this view, nor any support for it, neither from the language of the Arabs nor from the Sharia.

al-Khalil said: "Ash-shafaq" is the redness after the sun sets, and its redness is at the beginning of the night until near the late night prayer. The books of language and of the Sharia agree on this. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Arise, O boy, help me, not hesitating, against time, with a cup whose filling is shafaq."

And another said:

"Red in color, like the redness of the shafaq."

Mujahid said: "Ash-shafaq" is the whole day. Do you not see that He said: "and the night and what it gathers"? 'Ikrimah said: It is what remains of the day. They only said this because of His saying after it: "and the night and what it gathers," as if He swore by the light and the darkness. But there is no basis for this. Moreover, it has been related from 'Ikrimah that he said: "Ash-shafaq is what is between sunset and 'isha'." And it has been related from Asad ibn 'Amr: "The return."

"And the night and what it gathers." "Al-wasq" in the language of the scholars is gathering one thing to another. One says, "istawsaqat al-ibil," when the camels gathered and were brought together, and "al-ra'i yasiquha," meaning he gathers them.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes say: "and what it gathers and joins and contains and wraps." The meaning is that it gathers and joins what was scattered by day in its movement, because when the night comes every thing returns to its refuge. From it is the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi:

"Indeed I and you, and driving toward you, are like one who grasps a thing his fingers have not reached."

'Ikrimah said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it drives of anything to where it takes shelter," making it from driving (saw) and not from gathering. It was also said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it covers and conceals." It was also said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it carries," and whatever you carry, you have "wasaqta" it. The Arabs say: "I will not carry it, what my eye has wasaqat of water," meaning what it has carried. And "waseqat al-naqah tasiqu wasqan," meaning she carried a load.

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "wa ma waseq" and "what it carries" of darkness, or what it carries of the stars.

al-Qushayri said: The meaning of "hamala" is gathering and joining, and the night by its darkness carries every thing.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "wa ma waseq" means what is done in it of night prayer and seeking forgiveness at the dawns. The first is preferable.

﴿And the moon when it becomes full﴾, meaning it gathers and becomes complete.

al-Farra' said: Its "ittisaq" is its fullness, its gathering and its evenness on the thirteenth night and the fourteenth night, up to the sixteenth. It is formed from "wasq," which is gathering.

al-Hasan said: "ittasaqa" means it became full and gathered.

Qatadah said: "istadara," meaning it became round. One says, "wasaqtuhu fa-ittasaqa," as one says, "wasaltuhu fa-ittasala," and one says, "amr fulan muttasiq," meaning gathered and orderly. And one says, "ittasaqa al-shay'," when it followed in succession.

﴿You will surely ride from stage to stage﴾. This is the answer to the oath.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr read *la-tarkabanna* with a fatḥah on the bāʾ (the letter ب), taking it as addressed to one person, either the Prophet (ﷺ) or anyone suited to it. This is also the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Masrūq, Abū Wāʾil, Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. The rest read it with a ḍammah on the bāʾ, as address to the plural, namely the people.

Al-Shaʿbī and Mujāhid said: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, a heaven after a heaven." Al-Kalbī said: "That is, you will ascend through them." This applies to the first reading. It has also been said: a rank after a rank, and a station after a station, in nearness to God and elevation of status. It has also been said: the meaning is "you will pass through states, each state matching its fellow in severity." It has also been said: the meaning is "O human being, you will pass through states, from being a drop of sperm, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then living and dead, and rich and poor." In that case the address is to the human being mentioned in the words of God: ﴿O humankind, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second reading, saying: "Because the meaning is more fitting for people than for the Prophet (ﷺ)."

ʿUmar read *la-yarkabanna* with a yāʾ at the start (the letter ي) and a ḍammah on the bāʾ, as a statement about a third party. It is reported from him and from Ibn ʿAbbās that they read it with the third-person form and a fatḥah on the bāʾ, meaning: "*la-yarkabanna* al-insān (the human being will pass through states)." It is also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās that they read it with a kasrah on the letter of the present-tense prefix, which is a dialectal form. It was also read with a fatḥah on the letter of the present-tense prefix and a kasrah on the bāʾ, as address to the self.

It has been said that the meaning of the verse is: the moon will pass through states of waning and of new appearance. This is far-fetched.

Muqātil said: *ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, that is, death and life.

ʿIkrimah said: "Nursing infancy, then weaning, then boyhood, then youth, then old age."

The grammatical position of *ʿan ṭabaqin* is in the accusative, as it is a qualifier of *ṭabaqan*, meaning: a stage that goes beyond another stage. Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *la-tarkabunna*, meaning: going beyond, or "going beyond" in the singular.

﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ The interrogative is for denunciation, and the *fā'* (ف) indicates that what follows it, namely the denunciation and astonishment, is a consequence of what precedes it, namely the states of the Day of Resurrection or of other matters, according to the earlier disagreement. The meaning is: what is the matter with the disbelievers that they do not believe in Muḥammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought of the Qur'an, given the presence of what makes belief in it necessary?

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾. This conditional clause and its response are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning is: what prevents them from prostrating in humility when the Qur'an is recited?

Al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: "What is the matter with them that they do not pray?"

Abū Muslim said: the intended meaning is humility and submission.

It has been said that the intended meaning is the well-known prostration of recitation (*sujūd al-tilāwah*).

There has been disagreement over whether this place is one of the places of prostration during recitation or not. The evidence for prostration was given earlier, at the opening of this surah.

﴿Rather, those who disbelieve deny﴾, that is, they deny Muḥammad (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Book, which includes affirmation of the Oneness of God, the Resurrection, reward and punishment.

﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾, that is, what they hide within themselves of denial. Muqātil said: "They hide from their deeds."

Ibn Zayd said: "They gather from deeds, both righteous and evil." The word is derived from *al-wiʿāʾ* (the container in which something is gathered), and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"Goodness endures, though time be long upon it, / and evil is the foulest thing you have stored as provision."*

It is said: *waʿāhu*, meaning he memorized it; and *waʿaytu al-ḥadītha aʿīhi waʿyan*, meaning I took in the saying, and from it is God's words: ﴿an attentive ear﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 12].

﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾. That is: treat it as though it were good news for them, because His knowledge, glorified is He, of that in the manner mentioned necessitates their punishment. *Al-alīm* is the painful, the causer of pain. The speech comes in the manner of mockery toward them.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward never cut off﴾. This exception is disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*), meaning: but those who combined belief in God with righteous action, for them is a reward with God that is never cut off, that is, unbroken. It is said: *manantu al-ḥabla*, meaning I cut the rope. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"You see behind them, from the speed of the running, / dust-clouds like scattered particles."*

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-manīn* is dust, because it cuts off what is behind it. Every weak thing is *manīn* and *mamnūn*. It has been said that the meaning of *ghayra mamnūnin* is that it is not bestowed upon them as a favour. It is also permissible for the exception to be connected (*muttaṣil*), if what is meant is those among them who believed.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, regarding God's words ﴿When the heaven is split open﴾, that he said: "The heaven will be split open from the Milky Way."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it is right to do so﴾, that he said: "It listened when He spoke to it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also, regarding ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it is right to do so﴾, that he said: "It obeyed, and it is right to obey through obedience."

Al-Ḥākim reported from him and declared it sound, that he said: "It heard and obeyed." Regarding ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾, he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, and it casts out what is in it." He said: "It brings out what is in it of the dead and empties itself of them."

Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him, regarding ﴿and casts out what is in it﴾, that he said: "The gold bracelets."

Al-Ḥākim reported, and al-Suyūṭī said with a good chain, from Jābir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection the earth will be stretched like a hide, and then there will be for the son of Adam in it only the place of his two feet."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿You are toiling toward your Lord with toil﴾, that he said: "Working a work, and then meeting it," and he said: "meeting your deed."

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No one is called to account except that he is destroyed." I said: "Does not God say: ﴿Then as for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ ﴿he will be called to a light account﴾?" He said: "That is not the reckoning; rather, that is the presentation. Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is destroyed."

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh (p. 1603) reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say in some of his prayer: 'O God, call me to account with an easy reckoning.' When he had finished, I said: 'O Messenger of God, what is the easy reckoning?' He said: 'That he looks into his record and is pardoned for it. Indeed, whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is destroyed.'" In some wordings of the first hadith and this other hadith: "Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is punished."

Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ*, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Three things, whoever has them, God will call him to account with an easy reckoning and admit him to Paradise by His mercy: you give to one who withholds from you, you pardon one who wronged you, and you maintain ties with one who severed them from you."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding his words *yadʿū thubūran* (he calls out for destruction), that he said: "*al-Waylu*" (woe).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that regarding *innahu ẓanna an lan yaḥūra* (that he thought he would never return), he said: "He will be resurrected."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him: *an lan yaḥūra*, he said: "That he would never return."

Samawayh reported in his *Fawāʾid* from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "*al-Shafaq* is the redness."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbās.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "*Al-Shafaq* is the whole of the daytime."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding God's words ﴿and by the night and what it gathers﴾, that he said: "And what it enters into."

Abū ʿUbayd in his *Faḍāʾil*, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him *wa mā wasaq*: "And what it gathered."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him regarding God's words ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full﴾, that he said: "When it becomes level (*istawā*)."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Anbārī reported through several routes from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was asked about God's words ﴿and by the night and what it gathers﴾, and he said: "*Wa mā jamaʿa*" (and what it gathers). "Have you not heard his saying:

*'Indeed we have she-camels, lively and full, / gathering together, if only they found a driver.'*"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from him regarding ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full﴾ that he said: "The night of the thirteenth."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb regarding ﴿You will surely ride stage after stage﴾: "State after state." Al-Bukhārī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿You will surely ride stage after stage﴾: "State after state," and he said: "This is your Prophet (ﷺ)."

Abū ʿUbayd in *al-Qirāʾāt*, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Manīʿ, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he used to read *la-tarkabanna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, meaning with a fatḥah on the bāʾ of *tarkabanna*.

And he said: "That is, your Prophet (ﷺ), state after state."

Al-Ṭayālisī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī reported from him: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, the heaven, stage after stage."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim in *al-Kunā*, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Masʿūd that he read *la-tarkabanna*, meaning with a fatḥah on the bāʾ.

And he said: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, a heaven after a heaven."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* reported from him regarding *la-tarkabanna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, that he said: "That is, the heaven will split apart, then it will burst open, then it will turn red."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī reported from him also, regarding the verse, that he said: "The heaven will be like molten metal, and it will be rose-coloured like oil, and it will be frail, and it will be cracked open, so it will be stage after stage."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding God's words ﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾, that he said: "They keep it secret."

This is a Meccan surah without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Inshiqaq was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh related a similar report from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Rafi', who said: "I prayed the 'atamah (night) prayer behind Abu Hurayrah, and he recited ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and prostrated. I said to him, and he said: 'I prostrated behind Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ), and I will not stop prostrating in it until I meet him.'"

Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq].

Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Ruwayani in his Musnad, and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Buraydah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the noon prayer ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and similar surahs."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ is like His saying ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], in whether the verb is supplied or not.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: its splitting is one of the signs of the Resurrection, and the meaning of its splitting is its cleaving with white clouds, as in His saying ﴿and the day the sky is split open with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It was also said that it splits from the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is the gate of the sky.

Scholars differed about the answer (jawab) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). al-Farra' said that it is "adhinat" (it listened), and the waw is extra, and likewise "alqat" (it cast out). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the Arabs do not insert a waw except with ﴿hatta idha﴾ (until when), as in His saying ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and with ﴿lamma﴾ (when), as in His saying ﴿So when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead, and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104]; it is not inserted with anything other than these two.

It was said that the answer is His saying ﴿fa-mulaqihi﴾ (then you will meet it), meaning ﴿fa-anta mulaqihi﴾ (then you are one who will meet it), and this is the view of al-Akhfash.

al-Mubarrad said: In the speech there is a transposition, meaning ﴿O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet it﴾ ﴿when the sky splits open﴾.

al-Mubarrad also said: The answer is His saying ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾, and this is the view of al-Kisa'i. The construction is: ﴿when the sky splits open﴾, then whoever is given his record in his right hand, his ruling is such-and-such. It was also said that it is ﴿O mankind﴾ with the fa' (then) elided. It was said that it is ﴿O mankind﴾ with the saying elided, meaning it will be said to him, "O mankind." It was also said that the answer is omitted, its estimate being "you will be resurrected," or "every person will meet his deed." It was also said that it is what was stated in Surat al-Takwir, meaning "a soul will know this," on the assumption that ﴿idha﴾ is conditional. It was also said that it is not conditional, and it is governed by a deleted verb, meaning "remember," or it is a subject whose predicate is the second ﴿idha﴾, with the waw extra, and the estimate is: the time of the splitting of the sky is the time of the stretching of the earth.

The meaning of ﴿and it listened to its Lord﴾ is that it obeyed Him in splitting, from "idhn," which is listening to a thing and giving ear to it. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, meaning it is right for it to obey, submit and listen. Among the uses of "idhn" for listening is the poet's saying:

"Deaf, when they hear good said of me, and if I am mentioned with evil in their presence, they listen (adhinu)."

And the saying of another:

"If they listen to a doubt, they fly with it, rejoicing at me; and what they listen to of good is buried."

It was also said that the meaning is: Allah made it certain that it would listen to His command to split, meaning He made it fit for that.

al-Dahhak said: "Haqqat" means "it obeyed," and "it is right for it to obey its Lord because He created it." One says, "So-and-so is entitled (mahquq) to such-and-such." The meaning of its obedience is that it does not refuse what Allah wills for it.

Qatadah said: "It is right for it (haqqa laha) to do that." From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"If there is reproach, then welcome and hail; and reproach is due to her from us, and it has become scarce."

And ﴿when the earth is stretched out﴾, meaning spread out as hide is spread, and its mountains are leveled until it becomes a level plain in which you see no crookedness or elevation.

Muqatil said: It is made level like the stretching of a hide, so no building or mountain remains on it except that it enters into it. It was also said: "It is stretched" means its extent is increased, from "madad," which is increase.

﴿And it casts out what is in it﴾, meaning it brings out what is in it of the dead and the treasures, and throws them onto its surface, and empties itself of them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It casts out what is in its belly of the dead, and empties itself of those who are on its back of the living. Similar to this is His saying ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2].

﴿And it listened to its Lord﴾, meaning it heard and obeyed what He commanded it of casting out and emptying itself. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, meaning it was made fit for listening to that and submitting to it. The meaning of the two verbs has already been explained before this.

﴿O mankind﴾: the intended meaning is the human species, so it includes the believer and the disbeliever. It was also said that it refers only to the disbelieving human. The first is preferable because of the detail that will come. ﴿Indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil﴾. In the speech of the Arabs, "kadh" (toil) is striving at a thing with effort, without distinction between that thing being good or bad. The meaning is: indeed you are striving toward your Lord in your deed, or toward meeting your Lord. It is derived from "kadaha jildahu," meaning when he scratched his skin.

Ibn Muqbil said:

"Time is only two turns: in one of them I die, and in the other I seek life, toiling."

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: "Working for your Lord a work, then you will meet it," meaning you will meet your deed. The meaning is that you will inevitably meet the reward of your deed and what follows from it of reward and punishment.

al-Qutaybi said: The meaning of the verse is: indeed you are laboring, that is, working and toiling in your livelihood, toward the meeting with your Lord. "Mulaqah" means "liqa'," that is, you will meet your Lord with your deed. It was also said: "fa-mulaqin" means you will meet the book of your deed, because the deed has already ended.

﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾, and they are the believers.

﴿He will be brought to a reckoning that is easy﴾, one in which there is no scrutiny.

Muqatil said: Because his sins will be forgiven and he will not be brought to account for them.

The exegetes said: It is that his evil deeds are shown to him, then Allah forgives them, and that is the easy reckoning.

﴿And he will return to his people in happiness﴾, meaning after the easy reckoning he will return to his people who are in Paradise from among his kin, or to his people who were with him in the world of wives and children and who had preceded him to Paradise, or to those whom Allah has prepared for him in Paradise of the dark-eyed maidens (hur 'in) and the eternal youths, or to all of these, happy, rejoicing in what he has been given of goodness and honor.

﴿But as for he who is given his record behind his back﴾. al-Kalbi said: Because his right hand will be chained to his neck, and his left hand will be behind him.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: The bones and the plates of his chest will be unlocked, then his hand will enter and come out from his back, and he will take his record in that manner.

﴿He will call for destruction﴾, meaning when he reads his record he will say, "Woe to me! Destruction to me!" And "thubur" is ruin.

﴿And he will burn in the Blaze﴾, meaning he will enter it and suffer its heat and its severity.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and 'Asim read with a fat-hah on the ya' (yaṣla), a sukun on the sad and a light lam.

The rest read with a damma on the ya' and a fat-hah on the lam, with a shaddah. Isma'il al-Makki related from Ibn Kathir, and likewise Kharijah from Nafi', and likewise Isma'il al-Makki related from Ibn Kathir that they read with a damma on the ya' and a sukun on the sad, from "asla, yuslī."

﴿Indeed, he was among his people, happy﴾, meaning he was among his people in the world, happy in following his desire and indulging his lust, insolent and arrogant, because the Hereafter did not occur to his mind. The clause is a reason for what precedes it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return﴾ is a reason for his having been happy among his people in the world. The meaning is: the cause of that happiness was his supposing that he would not return to Allah and would not be raised for reckoning and punishment, because he denied the resurrection and rejected the Hereafter. The "an" in His saying ﴿an lan yahur﴾ (that he would never return) is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," which, with what follows it, takes the place of the two objects of "thanna" (supposed). "Haur" in language means return; one says "haara, yahuru" when he returns. al-Raghib said: "haur" is hesitation in a matter, and from it is the saying: "We seek refuge in Allah from haur after kawr," meaning from hesitation in a matter after proceeding in it. "Muhawarat al-kalam" is responding to speech, and "mahar" is the place of return and destination.

'Ikrimah and Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: "Yahur" is a word in Abyssinian, and its meaning is "return."

al-Qurtubi said: "Haur" in the speech of the Arabs is return, and from it is his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from haur after kawr," meaning from returning to deficiency after increase. Likewise "huur" with a damma. In the proverb: "haur in mahar," meaning a deficiency within a deficiency. From it is the saying of the poet:

"The blood is being poured out, and the people's return is in haur."

"Huur" is also destruction, and from it is the saying of the reciter:

"In a well of no haur he went, and he did not perceive."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: meaning "in a well of haur," and "la" is extra.

﴿Yes, indeed his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾. "Bala" is an affirmation of what was negated by "lan": meaning, yes, he will certainly return and will certainly be raised.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿indeed his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾, meaning He was aware of him and of his deeds, and nothing of them was hidden from Him.

al-Zajjaj said: "Kana bihi basiran" means He was seeing of him before He created him, knowing that his return was to Him.

﴿So I swear by the twilight﴾. The "la" is extra, as has been mentioned before in similar expressions, and we have already mentioned the disagreement about it in Surat al-Qiyamah, so refer back to it. "Ash-shafaq" is the redness that appears after the sun sets until the time of the late night prayer ('isha').

al-Wahidi said: This is the view of the exegetes and the lexicographers all together.

al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs say: "He has a dyed garment, as if it were the shafaq," and it was red. This is related by al-Qurtubi from most of the Companions, the Successors and the jurists.

Asad ibn 'Amr and Abu Hanifah, in one of the two reports from him, said: It is the whiteness. There is no basis for this view, nor any support for it, neither from the language of the Arabs nor from the Sharia.

al-Khalil said: "Ash-shafaq" is the redness after the sun sets, and its redness is at the beginning of the night until near the late night prayer. The books of language and of the Sharia agree on this. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Arise, O boy, help me, not hesitating, against time, with a cup whose filling is shafaq."

And another said:

"Red in color, like the redness of the shafaq."

Mujahid said: "Ash-shafaq" is the whole day. Do you not see that He said: "and the night and what it gathers"? 'Ikrimah said: It is what remains of the day. They only said this because of His saying after it: "and the night and what it gathers," as if He swore by the light and the darkness. But there is no basis for this. Moreover, it has been related from 'Ikrimah that he said: "Ash-shafaq is what is between sunset and 'isha'." And it has been related from Asad ibn 'Amr: "The return."

"And the night and what it gathers." "Al-wasq" in the language of the scholars is gathering one thing to another. One says, "istawsaqat al-ibil," when the camels gathered and were brought together, and "al-ra'i yasiquha," meaning he gathers them.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes say: "and what it gathers and joins and contains and wraps." The meaning is that it gathers and joins what was scattered by day in its movement, because when the night comes every thing returns to its refuge. From it is the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi:

"Indeed I and you, and driving toward you, are like one who grasps a thing his fingers have not reached."

'Ikrimah said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it drives of anything to where it takes shelter," making it from driving (saw) and not from gathering. It was also said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it covers and conceals." It was also said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it carries," and whatever you carry, you have "wasaqta" it. The Arabs say: "I will not carry it, what my eye has wasaqat of water," meaning what it has carried. And "waseqat al-naqah tasiqu wasqan," meaning she carried a load.

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "wa ma waseq" and "what it carries" of darkness, or what it carries of the stars.

al-Qushayri said: The meaning of "hamala" is gathering and joining, and the night by its darkness carries every thing.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "wa ma waseq" means what is done in it of night prayer and seeking forgiveness at the dawns. The first is preferable.

﴿And the moon when it becomes full﴾, meaning it gathers and becomes complete.

al-Farra' said: Its "ittisaq" is its fullness, its gathering and its evenness on the thirteenth night and the fourteenth night, up to the sixteenth. It is formed from "wasq," which is gathering.

al-Hasan said: "ittasaqa" means it became full and gathered.

Qatadah said: "istadara," meaning it became round. One says, "wasaqtuhu fa-ittasaqa," as one says, "wasaltuhu fa-ittasala," and one says, "amr fulan muttasiq," meaning gathered and orderly. And one says, "ittasaqa al-shay'," when it followed in succession.

﴿You will surely ride from stage to stage﴾. This is the answer to the oath.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr read *la-tarkabanna* with a fatḥah on the bāʾ (the letter ب), taking it as addressed to one person, either the Prophet (ﷺ) or anyone suited to it. This is also the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Masrūq, Abū Wāʾil, Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. The rest read it with a ḍammah on the bāʾ, as address to the plural, namely the people.

Al-Shaʿbī and Mujāhid said: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, a heaven after a heaven." Al-Kalbī said: "That is, you will ascend through them." This applies to the first reading. It has also been said: a rank after a rank, and a station after a station, in nearness to God and elevation of status. It has also been said: the meaning is "you will pass through states, each state matching its fellow in severity." It has also been said: the meaning is "O human being, you will pass through states, from being a drop of sperm, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then living and dead, and rich and poor." In that case the address is to the human being mentioned in the words of God: ﴿O humankind, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second reading, saying: "Because the meaning is more fitting for people than for the Prophet (ﷺ)."

ʿUmar read *la-yarkabanna* with a yāʾ at the start (the letter ي) and a ḍammah on the bāʾ, as a statement about a third party. It is reported from him and from Ibn ʿAbbās that they read it with the third-person form and a fatḥah on the bāʾ, meaning: "*la-yarkabanna* al-insān (the human being will pass through states)." It is also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās that they read it with a kasrah on the letter of the present-tense prefix, which is a dialectal form. It was also read with a fatḥah on the letter of the present-tense prefix and a kasrah on the bāʾ, as address to the self.

It has been said that the meaning of the verse is: the moon will pass through states of waning and of new appearance. This is far-fetched.

Muqātil said: *ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, that is, death and life.

ʿIkrimah said: "Nursing infancy, then weaning, then boyhood, then youth, then old age."

The grammatical position of *ʿan ṭabaqin* is in the accusative, as it is a qualifier of *ṭabaqan*, meaning: a stage that goes beyond another stage. Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *la-tarkabunna*, meaning: going beyond, or "going beyond" in the singular.

﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ The interrogative is for denunciation, and the *fā'* (ف) indicates that what follows it, namely the denunciation and astonishment, is a consequence of what precedes it, namely the states of the Day of Resurrection or of other matters, according to the earlier disagreement. The meaning is: what is the matter with the disbelievers that they do not believe in Muḥammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought of the Qur'an, given the presence of what makes belief in it necessary?

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾. This conditional clause and its response are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning is: what prevents them from prostrating in humility when the Qur'an is recited?

Al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: "What is the matter with them that they do not pray?"

Abū Muslim said: the intended meaning is humility and submission.

It has been said that the intended meaning is the well-known prostration of recitation (*sujūd al-tilāwah*).

There has been disagreement over whether this place is one of the places of prostration during recitation or not. The evidence for prostration was given earlier, at the opening of this surah.

﴿Rather, those who disbelieve deny﴾, that is, they deny Muḥammad (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Book, which includes affirmation of the Oneness of God, the Resurrection, reward and punishment.

﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾, that is, what they hide within themselves of denial. Muqātil said: "They hide from their deeds."

Ibn Zayd said: "They gather from deeds, both righteous and evil." The word is derived from *al-wiʿāʾ* (the container in which something is gathered), and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"Goodness endures, though time be long upon it, / and evil is the foulest thing you have stored as provision."*

It is said: *waʿāhu*, meaning he memorized it; and *waʿaytu al-ḥadītha aʿīhi waʿyan*, meaning I took in the saying, and from it is God's words: ﴿an attentive ear﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 12].

﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾. That is: treat it as though it were good news for them, because His knowledge, glorified is He, of that in the manner mentioned necessitates their punishment. *Al-alīm* is the painful, the causer of pain. The speech comes in the manner of mockery toward them.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward never cut off﴾. This exception is disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*), meaning: but those who combined belief in God with righteous action, for them is a reward with God that is never cut off, that is, unbroken. It is said: *manantu al-ḥabla*, meaning I cut the rope. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"You see behind them, from the speed of the running, / dust-clouds like scattered particles."*

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-manīn* is dust, because it cuts off what is behind it. Every weak thing is *manīn* and *mamnūn*. It has been said that the meaning of *ghayra mamnūnin* is that it is not bestowed upon them as a favour. It is also permissible for the exception to be connected (*muttaṣil*), if what is meant is those among them who believed.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, regarding God's words ﴿When the heaven is split open﴾, that he said: "The heaven will be split open from the Milky Way."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it is right to do so﴾, that he said: "It listened when He spoke to it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also, regarding ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it is right to do so﴾, that he said: "It obeyed, and it is right to obey through obedience."

Al-Ḥākim reported from him and declared it sound, that he said: "It heard and obeyed." Regarding ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾, he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, and it casts out what is in it." He said: "It brings out what is in it of the dead and empties itself of them."

Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him, regarding ﴿and casts out what is in it﴾, that he said: "The gold bracelets."

Al-Ḥākim reported, and al-Suyūṭī said with a good chain, from Jābir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection the earth will be stretched like a hide, and then there will be for the son of Adam in it only the place of his two feet."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿You are toiling toward your Lord with toil﴾, that he said: "Working a work, and then meeting it," and he said: "meeting your deed."

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No one is called to account except that he is destroyed." I said: "Does not God say: ﴿Then as for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ ﴿he will be called to a light account﴾?" He said: "That is not the reckoning; rather, that is the presentation. Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is destroyed."

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh (p. 1603) reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say in some of his prayer: 'O God, call me to account with an easy reckoning.' When he had finished, I said: 'O Messenger of God, what is the easy reckoning?' He said: 'That he looks into his record and is pardoned for it. Indeed, whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is destroyed.'" In some wordings of the first hadith and this other hadith: "Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is punished."

Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ*, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Three things, whoever has them, God will call him to account with an easy reckoning and admit him to Paradise by His mercy: you give to one who withholds from you, you pardon one who wronged you, and you maintain ties with one who severed them from you."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding his words *yadʿū thubūran* (he calls out for destruction), that he said: "*al-Waylu*" (woe).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that regarding *innahu ẓanna an lan yaḥūra* (that he thought he would never return), he said: "He will be resurrected."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him: *an lan yaḥūra*, he said: "That he would never return."

Samawayh reported in his *Fawāʾid* from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "*al-Shafaq* is the redness."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbās.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "*Al-Shafaq* is the whole of the daytime."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding God's words ﴿and by the night and what it gathers﴾, that he said: "And what it enters into."

Abū ʿUbayd in his *Faḍāʾil*, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him *wa mā wasaq*: "And what it gathered."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him regarding God's words ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full﴾, that he said: "When it becomes level (*istawā*)."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Anbārī reported through several routes from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was asked about God's words ﴿and by the night and what it gathers﴾, and he said: "*Wa mā jamaʿa*" (and what it gathers). "Have you not heard his saying:

*'Indeed we have she-camels, lively and full, / gathering together, if only they found a driver.'*"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from him regarding ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full﴾ that he said: "The night of the thirteenth."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb regarding ﴿You will surely ride stage after stage﴾: "State after state." Al-Bukhārī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿You will surely ride stage after stage﴾: "State after state," and he said: "This is your Prophet (ﷺ)."

Abū ʿUbayd in *al-Qirāʾāt*, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Manīʿ, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he used to read *la-tarkabanna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, meaning with a fatḥah on the bāʾ of *tarkabanna*.

And he said: "That is, your Prophet (ﷺ), state after state."

Al-Ṭayālisī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī reported from him: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, the heaven, stage after stage."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim in *al-Kunā*, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Masʿūd that he read *la-tarkabanna*, meaning with a fatḥah on the bāʾ.

And he said: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, a heaven after a heaven."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* reported from him regarding *la-tarkabanna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, that he said: "That is, the heaven will split apart, then it will burst open, then it will turn red."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqī reported from him also, regarding the verse, that he said: "The heaven will be like molten metal, and it will be rose-coloured like oil, and it will be frail, and it will be cracked open, so it will be stage after stage."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding God's words ﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾, that he said: "They keep it secret."

This is a Meccan surah without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Inshiqaq was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh related a similar report from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Rafi', who said: "I prayed the 'atamah (night) prayer behind Abu Hurayrah, and he recited ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and prostrated. I said to him, and he said: 'I prostrated behind Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ), and I will not stop prostrating in it until I meet him.'"

Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "We prostrated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾" [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq].

Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Ruwayani in his Musnad, and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi in al-Mukhtarah related from Buraydah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the noon prayer ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ and similar surahs."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ is like His saying ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1], in whether the verb is supplied or not.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: its splitting is one of the signs of the Resurrection, and the meaning of its splitting is its cleaving with white clouds, as in His saying ﴿and the day the sky is split open with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It was also said that it splits from the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is the gate of the sky.

Scholars differed about the answer (jawab) of ﴿idha﴾ (when). al-Farra' said that it is "adhinat" (it listened), and the waw is extra, and likewise "alqat" (it cast out). Ibn al-Anbari said: This is an error, because the Arabs do not insert a waw except with ﴿hatta idha﴾ (until when), as in His saying ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], and with ﴿lamma﴾ (when), as in His saying ﴿So when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead, and We called to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–104]; it is not inserted with anything other than these two.

It was said that the answer is His saying ﴿fa-mulaqihi﴾ (then you will meet it), meaning ﴿fa-anta mulaqihi﴾ (then you are one who will meet it), and this is the view of al-Akhfash.

al-Mubarrad said: In the speech there is a transposition, meaning ﴿O mankind, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet it﴾ ﴿when the sky splits open﴾.

al-Mubarrad also said: The answer is His saying ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾, and this is the view of al-Kisa'i. The construction is: ﴿when the sky splits open﴾, then whoever is given his record in his right hand, his ruling is such-and-such. It was also said that it is ﴿O mankind﴾ with the fa' (then) elided. It was said that it is ﴿O mankind﴾ with the saying elided, meaning it will be said to him, "O mankind." It was also said that the answer is omitted, its estimate being "you will be resurrected," or "every person will meet his deed." It was also said that it is what was stated in Surat al-Takwir, meaning "a soul will know this," on the assumption that ﴿idha﴾ is conditional. It was also said that it is not conditional, and it is governed by a deleted verb, meaning "remember," or it is a subject whose predicate is the second ﴿idha﴾, with the waw extra, and the estimate is: the time of the splitting of the sky is the time of the stretching of the earth.

The meaning of ﴿and it listened to its Lord﴾ is that it obeyed Him in splitting, from "idhn," which is listening to a thing and giving ear to it. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, meaning it is right for it to obey, submit and listen. Among the uses of "idhn" for listening is the poet's saying:

"Deaf, when they hear good said of me, and if I am mentioned with evil in their presence, they listen (adhinu)."

And the saying of another:

"If they listen to a doubt, they fly with it, rejoicing at me; and what they listen to of good is buried."

It was also said that the meaning is: Allah made it certain that it would listen to His command to split, meaning He made it fit for that.

al-Dahhak said: "Haqqat" means "it obeyed," and "it is right for it to obey its Lord because He created it." One says, "So-and-so is entitled (mahquq) to such-and-such." The meaning of its obedience is that it does not refuse what Allah wills for it.

Qatadah said: "It is right for it (haqqa laha) to do that." From this is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"If there is reproach, then welcome and hail; and reproach is due to her from us, and it has become scarce."

And ﴿when the earth is stretched out﴾, meaning spread out as hide is spread, and its mountains are leveled until it becomes a level plain in which you see no crookedness or elevation.

Muqatil said: It is made level like the stretching of a hide, so no building or mountain remains on it except that it enters into it. It was also said: "It is stretched" means its extent is increased, from "madad," which is increase.

﴿And it casts out what is in it﴾, meaning it brings out what is in it of the dead and the treasures, and throws them onto its surface, and empties itself of them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It casts out what is in its belly of the dead, and empties itself of those who are on its back of the living. Similar to this is His saying ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2].

﴿And it listened to its Lord﴾, meaning it heard and obeyed what He commanded it of casting out and emptying itself. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, meaning it was made fit for listening to that and submitting to it. The meaning of the two verbs has already been explained before this.

﴿O mankind﴾: the intended meaning is the human species, so it includes the believer and the disbeliever. It was also said that it refers only to the disbelieving human. The first is preferable because of the detail that will come. ﴿Indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil﴾. In the speech of the Arabs, "kadh" (toil) is striving at a thing with effort, without distinction between that thing being good or bad. The meaning is: indeed you are striving toward your Lord in your deed, or toward meeting your Lord. It is derived from "kadaha jildahu," meaning when he scratched his skin.

Ibn Muqbil said:

"Time is only two turns: in one of them I die, and in the other I seek life, toiling."

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: "Working for your Lord a work, then you will meet it," meaning you will meet your deed. The meaning is that you will inevitably meet the reward of your deed and what follows from it of reward and punishment.

al-Qutaybi said: The meaning of the verse is: indeed you are laboring, that is, working and toiling in your livelihood, toward the meeting with your Lord. "Mulaqah" means "liqa'," that is, you will meet your Lord with your deed. It was also said: "fa-mulaqin" means you will meet the book of your deed, because the deed has already ended.

﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand﴾, and they are the believers.

﴿He will be brought to a reckoning that is easy﴾, one in which there is no scrutiny.

Muqatil said: Because his sins will be forgiven and he will not be brought to account for them.

The exegetes said: It is that his evil deeds are shown to him, then Allah forgives them, and that is the easy reckoning.

﴿And he will return to his people in happiness﴾, meaning after the easy reckoning he will return to his people who are in Paradise from among his kin, or to his people who were with him in the world of wives and children and who had preceded him to Paradise, or to those whom Allah has prepared for him in Paradise of the dark-eyed maidens (hur 'in) and the eternal youths, or to all of these, happy, rejoicing in what he has been given of goodness and honor.

﴿But as for he who is given his record behind his back﴾. al-Kalbi said: Because his right hand will be chained to his neck, and his left hand will be behind him.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: The bones and the plates of his chest will be unlocked, then his hand will enter and come out from his back, and he will take his record in that manner.

﴿He will call for destruction﴾, meaning when he reads his record he will say, "Woe to me! Destruction to me!" And "thubur" is ruin.

﴿And he will burn in the Blaze﴾, meaning he will enter it and suffer its heat and its severity.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and 'Asim read with a fat-hah on the ya' (yaṣla), a sukun on the sad and a light lam.

The rest read with a damma on the ya' and a fat-hah on the lam, with a shaddah. Isma'il al-Makki related from Ibn Kathir, and likewise Kharijah from Nafi', and likewise Isma'il al-Makki related from Ibn Kathir that they read with a damma on the ya' and a sukun on the sad, from "asla, yuslī."

﴿Indeed, he was among his people, happy﴾, meaning he was among his people in the world, happy in following his desire and indulging his lust, insolent and arrogant, because the Hereafter did not occur to his mind. The clause is a reason for what precedes it.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return﴾ is a reason for his having been happy among his people in the world. The meaning is: the cause of that happiness was his supposing that he would not return to Allah and would not be raised for reckoning and punishment, because he denied the resurrection and rejected the Hereafter. The "an" in His saying ﴿an lan yahur﴾ (that he would never return) is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," which, with what follows it, takes the place of the two objects of "thanna" (supposed). "Haur" in language means return; one says "haara, yahuru" when he returns. al-Raghib said: "haur" is hesitation in a matter, and from it is the saying: "We seek refuge in Allah from haur after kawr," meaning from hesitation in a matter after proceeding in it. "Muhawarat al-kalam" is responding to speech, and "mahar" is the place of return and destination.

'Ikrimah and Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: "Yahur" is a word in Abyssinian, and its meaning is "return."

al-Qurtubi said: "Haur" in the speech of the Arabs is return, and from it is his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from haur after kawr," meaning from returning to deficiency after increase. Likewise "huur" with a damma. In the proverb: "haur in mahar," meaning a deficiency within a deficiency. From it is the saying of the poet:

"The blood is being poured out, and the people's return is in haur."

"Huur" is also destruction, and from it is the saying of the reciter:

"In a well of no haur he went, and he did not perceive."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: meaning "in a well of haur," and "la" is extra.

﴿Yes, indeed his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾. "Bala" is an affirmation of what was negated by "lan": meaning, yes, he will certainly return and will certainly be raised.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿indeed his Lord was ever seeing of him﴾, meaning He was aware of him and of his deeds, and nothing of them was hidden from Him.

al-Zajjaj said: "Kana bihi basiran" means He was seeing of him before He created him, knowing that his return was to Him.

﴿So I swear by the twilight﴾. The "la" is extra, as has been mentioned before in similar expressions, and we have already mentioned the disagreement about it in Surat al-Qiyamah, so refer back to it. "Ash-shafaq" is the redness that appears after the sun sets until the time of the late night prayer ('isha').

al-Wahidi said: This is the view of the exegetes and the lexicographers all together.

al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs say: "He has a dyed garment, as if it were the shafaq," and it was red. This is related by al-Qurtubi from most of the Companions, the Successors and the jurists.

Asad ibn 'Amr and Abu Hanifah, in one of the two reports from him, said: It is the whiteness. There is no basis for this view, nor any support for it, neither from the language of the Arabs nor from the Sharia.

al-Khalil said: "Ash-shafaq" is the redness after the sun sets, and its redness is at the beginning of the night until near the late night prayer. The books of language and of the Sharia agree on this. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Arise, O boy, help me, not hesitating, against time, with a cup whose filling is shafaq."

And another said:

"Red in color, like the redness of the shafaq."

Mujahid said: "Ash-shafaq" is the whole day. Do you not see that He said: "and the night and what it gathers"? 'Ikrimah said: It is what remains of the day. They only said this because of His saying after it: "and the night and what it gathers," as if He swore by the light and the darkness. But there is no basis for this. Moreover, it has been related from 'Ikrimah that he said: "Ash-shafaq is what is between sunset and 'isha'." And it has been related from Asad ibn 'Amr: "The return."

"And the night and what it gathers." "Al-wasq" in the language of the scholars is gathering one thing to another. One says, "istawsaqat al-ibil," when the camels gathered and were brought together, and "al-ra'i yasiquha," meaning he gathers them.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes say: "and what it gathers and joins and contains and wraps." The meaning is that it gathers and joins what was scattered by day in its movement, because when the night comes every thing returns to its refuge. From it is the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi:

"Indeed I and you, and driving toward you, are like one who grasps a thing his fingers have not reached."

'Ikrimah said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it drives of anything to where it takes shelter," making it from driving (saw) and not from gathering. It was also said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it covers and conceals." It was also said: "wa ma waseq" means "and what it carries," and whatever you carry, you have "wasaqta" it. The Arabs say: "I will not carry it, what my eye has wasaqat of water," meaning what it has carried. And "waseqat al-naqah tasiqu wasqan," meaning she carried a load.

Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "wa ma waseq" and "what it carries" of darkness, or what it carries of the stars.

al-Qushayri said: The meaning of "hamala" is gathering and joining, and the night by its darkness carries every thing.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "wa ma waseq" means what is done in it of night prayer and seeking forgiveness at the dawns. The first is preferable.

﴿And the moon when it becomes full﴾, meaning it gathers and becomes complete.

al-Farra' said: Its "ittisaq" is its fullness, its gathering and its evenness on the thirteenth night and the fourteenth night, up to the sixteenth. It is formed from "wasq," which is gathering.

al-Hasan said: "ittasaqa" means it became full and gathered.

Qatadah said: "istadara," meaning it became round. One says, "wasaqtuhu fa-ittasaqa," as one says, "wasaltuhu fa-ittasala," and one says, "amr fulan muttasiq," meaning gathered and orderly. And one says, "ittasaqa al-shay'," when it followed in succession.

﴿You will surely ride from stage to stage﴾. This is the answer to the oath.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr read *la-tarkabanna* with a fatḥah on the bāʾ (the letter ب), taking it as addressed to one person, either the Prophet (ﷺ) or anyone suited to it. This is also the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Masrūq, Abū Wāʾil, Mujāhid, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. The rest read it with a ḍammah on the bāʾ, as address to the plural, namely the people.

Al-Shaʿbī and Mujāhid said: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, a heaven after a heaven." Al-Kalbī said: "That is, you will ascend through them." This applies to the first reading. It has also been said: a rank after a rank, and a station after a station, in nearness to God and elevation of status. It has also been said: the meaning is "you will pass through states, each state matching its fellow in severity." It has also been said: the meaning is "O human being, you will pass through states, from being a drop of sperm, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then living and dead, and rich and poor." In that case the address is to the human being mentioned in the words of God: ﴿O humankind, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾. Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim preferred the second reading, saying: "Because the meaning is more fitting for people than for the Prophet (ﷺ)."

ʿUmar read *la-yarkabanna* with a yāʾ at the start (the letter ي) and a ḍammah on the bāʾ, as a statement about a third party. It is reported from him and from Ibn ʿAbbās that they read it with the third-person form and a fatḥah on the bāʾ, meaning: "*la-yarkabanna* al-insān (the human being will pass through states)." It is also reported from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās that they read it with a kasrah on the letter of the present-tense prefix, which is a dialectal form. It was also read with a fatḥah on the letter of the present-tense prefix and a kasrah on the bāʾ, as address to the self.

It has been said that the meaning of the verse is: the moon will pass through states of waning and of new appearance. This is far-fetched.

Muqātil said: *ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, that is, death and life.

ʿIkrimah said: "Nursing infancy, then weaning, then boyhood, then youth, then old age."

The grammatical position of *ʿan ṭabaqin* is in the accusative, as it is a qualifier of *ṭabaqan*, meaning: a stage that goes beyond another stage. Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *la-tarkabunna*, meaning: going beyond, or "going beyond" in the singular.

﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ The interrogative is for denunciation, and the *fā'* (ف) indicates that what follows it, namely the denunciation and astonishment, is a consequence of what precedes it, namely the states of the Day of Resurrection or of other matters, according to the earlier disagreement. The meaning is: what is the matter with the disbelievers that they do not believe in Muḥammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought of the Qur'an, given the presence of what makes belief in it necessary?

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾. This conditional clause and its response are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning is: what prevents them from prostrating in humility when the Qur'an is recited?

Al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: "What is the matter with them that they do not pray?"

Abū Muslim said: the intended meaning is humility and submission.

It has been said that the intended meaning is the well-known prostration of recitation (*sujūd al-tilāwah*).

There has been disagreement over whether this place is one of the places of prostration during recitation or not. The evidence for prostration was given earlier, at the opening of this surah.

﴿Rather, those who disbelieve deny﴾, that is, they deny Muḥammad (ﷺ) and what he brought of the Book, which includes affirmation of the Oneness of God, the Resurrection, reward and punishment.

﴿And God knows best what they conceal﴾, that is, what they hide within themselves of denial. Muqātil said: "They hide from their deeds."

Ibn Zayd said: "They gather from deeds, both righteous and evil." The word is derived from *al-wiʿāʾ* (the container in which something is gathered), and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"Goodness endures, though time be long upon it, / and evil is the foulest thing you have stored as provision."*

It is said: *waʿāhu*, meaning he memorized it; and *waʿaytu al-ḥadītha aʿīhi waʿyan*, meaning I took in the saying, and from it is God's words: ﴿an attentive ear﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 12].

﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾. That is: treat it as though it were good news for them, because His knowledge, glorified is He, of that in the manner mentioned necessitates their punishment. *Al-alīm* is the painful, the causer of pain. The speech comes in the manner of mockery toward them.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward never cut off﴾. This exception is disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*), meaning: but those who combined belief in God with righteous action, for them is a reward with God that is never cut off, that is, unbroken. It is said: *manantu al-ḥabla*, meaning I cut the rope. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"You see behind them, from the speed of the running, / dust-clouds like scattered particles."*

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-manīn* is dust, because it cuts off what is behind it. Every weak thing is *manīn* and *mamnūn*. It has been said that the meaning of *ghayra mamnūnin* is that it is not bestowed upon them as a favour. It is also permissible for the exception to be connected (*muttaṣil*), if what is meant is those among them who believed.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, regarding God's words ﴿When the heaven is split open﴾, that he said: "The heaven will be split open from the Milky Way."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it is right to do so﴾, that he said: "It listened when He spoke to it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also, regarding ﴿And it has listened to its Lord and it is right to do so﴾, that he said: "It obeyed, and it is right to obey through obedience."

Al-Ḥākim reported from him and declared it sound, that he said: "It heard and obeyed." Regarding ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾, he said: "On the Day of Resurrection, and it casts out what is in it." He said: "It brings out what is in it of the dead and empties itself of them."

Ibn al-Mundhir also reported from him, regarding ﴿and casts out what is in it﴾, that he said: "The gold bracelets."

Al-Ḥākim reported, and al-Suyūṭī said with a good chain, from Jābir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection the earth will be stretched like a hide, and then there will be for the son of Adam in it only the place of his two feet."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿You are toiling toward your Lord with toil﴾, that he said: "Working a work, and then meeting it," and he said: "meeting your deed."

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No one is called to account except that he is destroyed." I said: "Does not God say: ﴿Then as for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ ﴿he will be called to a light account﴾?" He said: "That is not the reckoning; rather, that is the presentation. Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is destroyed."

Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ḥākim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh (p. 1603) reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say in some of his prayer: 'O God, call me to account with an easy reckoning.' When he had finished, I said: 'O Messenger of God, what is the easy reckoning?' He said: 'That he looks into his record and is pardoned for it. Indeed, whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is destroyed.'" In some wordings of the first hadith and this other hadith: "Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised is punished."

Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Awsaṭ*, al-Bayhaqī and al-Ḥākim reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Three things, whoever has them, God will call him to account with an easy reckoning and admit him to Paradise by His mercy: you give to one who withholds from you, you pardon one who wronged you, and you maintain ties with one who severed them from you."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding his words *yadʿū thubūran* (he calls out for destruction), that he said: "*al-Waylu*" (woe).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him that regarding *innahu ẓanna an lan yaḥūra* (that he thought he would never return), he said: "He will be resurrected."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him: *an lan yaḥūra*, he said: "That he would never return."

Samawayh reported in his *Fawāʾid* from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who said: "*al-Shafaq* is the redness."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbās.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "*Al-Shafaq* is the whole of the daytime."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding God's words ﴿and by the night and what it gathers﴾, that he said: "And what it enters into."

Abū ʿUbayd in his *Faḍāʾil*, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him *wa mā wasaq*: "And what it gathered."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him regarding God's words ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full﴾, that he said: "When it becomes level (*istawā*)."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Anbārī reported through several routes from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was asked about God's words ﴿and by the night and what it gathers﴾, and he said: "*Wa mā jamaʿa*" (and what it gathers). "Have you not heard his saying:

*'Indeed we have she-camels, lively and full, / gathering together, if only they found a driver.'*"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from him regarding ﴿and by the moon when it becomes full﴾ that he said: "The night of the thirteenth."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb regarding ﴿You will surely ride stage after stage﴾: "State after state." Al-Bukhārī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿You will surely ride stage after stage﴾: "State after state," and he said: "This is your Prophet (ﷺ)."

Abū ʿUbayd in *al-Qirāʾāt*, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Manīʿ, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he used to read *la-tarkabanna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaqin*, meaning with a fatḥah on the bāʾ of *tarkabanna*.

And he said: "That is, your Prophet (ﷺ), state after state."

Al-Ṭayālisī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī reported from him: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, the heaven, stage after stage."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim in *al-Kunā*, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mandah and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Masʿūd that he read *la-tarkabanna*, meaning with a fatḥah on the bāʾ.

And he said: "*La-tarkabanna*, O Muḥammad, a heaven after a heaven."
